geologicalDateSource: International Commission on Stratigraphy chart, version 2026/06. Values below use this chart rather than older rounded ranges still printed on museum pages.
scope: Twelve records cover all eight requested geological labels and four requested civilizations. Civilization entries deliberately focus on particular periods rather than flattening their whole histories.

events.title: Classical Greece: art, politics and power
events.summary: Greek city-states produced influential forms of art and public life during the Classical period. Athens's cultural achievements were also tied to military alliances and imperial wealth, making this a chapter of political competition as well as artistic experimentation.
events.sourceTitle: The Art of Classical Greece — Metropolitan Museum of Art
events.detail: The Delian League began as an alliance but became increasingly subject to Athens. Greek sculpture and architecture explored idealized bodies, balance and naturalistic representation; later Roman copies preserve evidence of many lost Greek originals.
events.nuance: The range describes Classical Greece, not all ancient Greek history. Athens was not all Greece, and ancient citizenship excluded many residents. Cultural achievements coexisted with slavery, warfare and empire.

events.title: Han China: an empire of institutions and exchange
events.summary: The Han dynasty reunited China after the collapse of Qin rule and developed cities, state institutions and a flourishing literary culture. Trade and diplomacy connected the empire with Central Asia and beyond, while technology and scholarship helped shape later traditions of Chinese statecraft.
people: Han officials, artisans, traders and farmers
events.sourceTitle: Han Dynasty — Metropolitan Museum of Art
events.detail: Sima Qian's Historical Records became an influential model for later histories. Confucian writings helped shape official education, and material evidence documents developments in paper, astronomy and other technologies.
events.nuance: Han is one chapter of Chinese civilization, not its origin. The dynasty included Western and Eastern phases separated by an interruption; some chronologies use 202 BCE as its political founding rather than the Met's 206 BCE. Territorial expansion involved conquest as well as exchange.
events.confidence: high; founding date varies with convention

events.title: The Indus civilization: the ingenuity of everyday cities
events.summary: Cities of the Indus civilization developed substantial housing, drainage and water infrastructure across the northwestern Indian subcontinent. Seals, standardized objects and long-distance contacts reveal an organized urban world whose achievements were closely connected to everyday life and trade.
events.sourceTitle: Art of the First Cities — Metropolitan Museum of Art
events.detail: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are among its best-known cities. Short inscriptions on stone seals attest to a sign system that remains undeciphered, limiting what can be said confidently about named rulers, language and political organization.
events.nuance: This is the Mature Harappan period, not the whole history of India or the Indus tradition. Its territory crossed today's India–Pakistan border, and major sites are in both countries. Avoid inventing kings, translating undeciphered inscriptions, or assuming all urban design proves one centralized government.
events.confidence: high for material evidence; political and linguistic interpretations unresolved

events.title: Uruk: the city and the written record
events.summary: Uruk grew into a major city in southern Mesopotamia with monumental mud-brick buildings and complex administration. Pictographs on clay recorded goods and workers' rations, showing how managing urban life helped develop the precursors of cuneiform writing.
events.sourceTitle: Uruk: The First City — Metropolitan Museum of Art
events.detail: Southern Mesopotamia lies largely in present-day Iraq. Art, seals and tablets preserve relationships among economic organization, religious institutions and authority, while imported materials show links beyond the city.
events.nuance: The display range identifies late-fourth-millennium urbanization, not all Mesopotamian history. Uruk was among the earliest major cities; an absolute single 'first city' depends on definitions and evidence. Gilgamesh traditions concern a later period and should not be treated as verified eyewitness history here.

events.title: Permian: life before the Great Dying
events.summary: Before dinosaurs dominated, Paleozoic land ecosystems included a wide range of synapsids and other animals. The end-Permian extinction devastated life on land and in the seas, marking the transition to the Mesozoic and a long period of ecological recovery.
events.sourceTitle: The Triassic Period: the rise of dinosaurs — Natural History Museum
events.detail: The extinction boundary separates the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras. Its profound impact is one reason scientists examine how major environmental changes interact with ecosystems.
events.nuance: Do not confuse the end-Permian event with the asteroid extinction at 66 million years. Synapsids are the lineage that includes mammals; the older phrase mammal-like reptiles is potentially misleading. Avoid an unsupported precise percentage or a single-cause claim.
events.confidence: high for period boundaries and broad ecological change

events.title: Carboniferous: wetlands and immense arthropods
events.summary: Carboniferous landscapes included extensive wetlands and forests, alongside animals such as giant millipedes and dragonfly-like griffinflies. Fossils from these environments reveal a striking world that existed long before the first dinosaurs.
events.sourceTitle: The world's largest arthropod was a car-sized millipede — Natural History Museum
events.detail: Coal measures preserve evidence of many ancient plants. Arthropleura fossils show that some terrestrial arthropods reached extraordinary sizes; griffinflies were a separate extinct group resembling modern dragonflies.
events.nuance: The whole planet was not one swamp. Higher oxygen is one proposed contributor to arthropod gigantism, not a complete settled explanation. Carboniferous includes the Mississippian and Pennsylvanian subdivisions.

events.title: Devonian: fins at the edge of land
events.summary: During the Devonian, many major fish groups diversified, and vertebrates began the long transition toward life on land. Fossils such as Tiktaalik preserve combinations of fish and four-limbed-animal features, helping researchers reconstruct evolutionary change rather than imagine one sudden leap.
people: paleontologists studying fish and early tetrapods (modern investigators)
events.sourceTitle: Prehistoric fish: significant species — Natural History Museum
events.detail: Tiktaalik had scales, gills and fins as well as a mobile neck and limb bones comparable to those of later tetrapods. Such mosaics of characteristics show how structures were modified over generations.
events.nuance: Tiktaalik should not be confidently labeled the single direct ancestor of all land vertebrates, nor the first creature ever on land. Plants and arthropods had terrestrial histories earlier; evolution forms branching lineages.

events.title: Silurian: the land gains living structure
events.summary: The Silurian fossil record documents early vascular plants and an expanding history of organisms on land. These small pioneers help explain how terrestrial ecosystems developed long before forests and flowering plants familiar today.
events.sourceTitle: Reading the rocks — Natural History Museum

additionalSources.title: Silurian Period — US National Park Service

events.detail: Fossil evidence and comparisons with living plants are used to investigate the origins of plant organs and tissue systems. Changes in sea level and sediment preservation influence which parts of this history are recoverable.
events.nuance: The first evidence of land plants predates the Silurian; this chapter emphasizes early vascular plants and diversification. Do not populate scenes with modern flowers or trees. The NPS page prints older boundary estimates; use the ICS 2026 range supplied here.
events.confidence: high for broad transition; earliest evidence continues to be revised

events.title: Ordovician: the oceans diversify
events.summary: Ordovician seas supported diversifying marine communities, including brachiopods, trilobites and other invertebrates. Near the period's end, extensive glaciation and falling sea levels accompanied a mass extinction that profoundly affected marine life.
events.sourceTitle: Ordovician Period — US National Park Service
events.detail: Shallow-water habitats were sensitive to changes in sea level. The fossil record allows scientists to compare communities before and after this major interruption in biodiversity.
events.nuance: The record does not show every organism or habitat equally. Avoid one exact global species-loss percentage. The NPS page uses older numerical boundaries; the supplied range follows the current ICS chart.

events.title: Cambrian: ecosystems become more complex
events.summary: In the Cambrian, animal diversity expanded dramatically in the fossil record, with many major body plans, hard parts and ecological relationships becoming conspicuous. Sites such as the Burgess Shale and Chengjiang preserve exceptional glimpses of these ancient marine communities.
events.sourceTitle: The Cambrian Period — Natural History Museum
events.detail: Shells, spines and burrowing behavior changed interactions among organisms and their environments. Fossils with exceptional soft-tissue preservation reveal much that ordinary shells and fragments cannot.
events.nuance: The Cambrian explosion lasted millions of years and had Precambrian foundations; it did not create all life instantaneously. The Cambrian is a period, not an epoch, and its animals should not be portrayed as dinosaurs.

events.title: Ediacaran: unfamiliar lives on ancient seafloors
events.summary: Ediacaran rocks preserve unusual organisms with frond-like, ribbon-like and other unfamiliar forms. Their traces offer a view of ecosystems before the better-known Cambrian communities and raise questions about how early animal life related to later lineages.
people: Douglas Erwin and other paleobiologists (modern investigators)
events.sourceTitle: History of Life on Earth — Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
events.detail: Fossils and movement traces help researchers investigate behavior and biological relationships. Many Ediacaran forms do not fit neatly into familiar modern groups.
events.nuance: Not every Ediacaran fossil is securely assigned to an animal lineage. The date range names the geological period, not the exact first appearance of each organism. Older museum text rounds the ending to 541 million; use the current ICS boundary here.
events.confidence: high for record and boundaries; biological relationships remain debated

events.title: Precambrian: most of Earth's story
events.summary: Before the Cambrian, Earth passed through billions of years of planetary, atmospheric and biological change. Microbial life and the later rise of oxygen transformed environments long before the appearance of abundant animal fossils, building conditions on which later ecosystems depended.
events.sourceTitle: Proterozoic Eon — US National Park Service
events.detail: Precambrian is a broad informal umbrella for the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic eons. The Ediacaran is its final formal period, so these labels are nested rather than separate non-overlapping units.
events.nuance: Precambrian is not one formal geological period. The 4540-million-year starting value is a rounded estimate for Earth's age; the ICS Hadean starts at the solar-system reference age 4567 million years. Do not merge first microbes, atmospheric oxygenation and animal origins into one event.
